The town of Jaffna is located in the northern part of Sri Lanka. However, this small town has played a major role in many wars that have taken place around the world.
Jaffna was once an important trading center for spices and other goods from India to Europe. The Portuguese were the first Europeans to arrive here in 1505. They built a fort on the island of Nainativu (Delft) off the coast of Jaffna. In 1619, the Dutch took over the area from the Portuguese. During their rule, they constructed several forts including one at Karaitivu (Ceylon). After the British defeated them in battle, they became rulers of Ceylon until independence in 1948.
In World War II, Japanese forces invaded Malaya and Singapore but failed to capture these two islands because of strong resistance by local troops supported by Allied air power. As a result, most of the Japanese army retreated back into Burma where they faced stiff opposition from Chinese guerrillas who had been trained by American pilots flying B-25 bombers out of China's Yunnan province. This forced Japan to withdraw its remaining soldiers from Southeast Asia before it could complete its conquests there.
After the war ended, Britain granted independence to all its colonies except Hong Kong which remained under British control until 1997 when it returned to China as part of a deal between London and Beijing. At this time, Jaffna was still ruled by the British government through its colonial administration known as "the Crown Colony" or simply "Colony." It consisted mainly of Tamil-speaking people living along coastal areas near Colombo port city while Sinhalese lived inland away from sea shores due to fear of pirates attacking ships carrying cargo across Indian Ocean waters during monsoon season every year between June & September months each year depending upon weather conditions prevailing then!
During the Second World War, Jaffna was occupied by the Japanese Army. The occupation lasted only three days, but it left behind a legacy of destruction and suffering. The Japanese killed thousands of civilians and destroyed much property in their brief stay. Many more died later after being deported to work camps in Thailand and elsewhere.
The Japanese also used Jaffna as a base for attacks against nearby countries such as Australia and New Zealand. These raids caused great damage to both nations' economies

The position of women in the history of Tamil literature in Sri Lanka
This article is a translation of an essay written by Dr. Sivapalan, who was born and brought up in Jaffna. He has been living in Canada since 1988.
In this article I will discuss the status of women in the history of Tamil literature in Sri Lanka. The first question that arises here is: what do we mean when we say “Tamil Literature”? Do we refer to all works written in Tamil? Or only those which are considered as literary classics?
If it were possible for us to answer these questions with certainty, then there would be no need for me to write about them at length. But unfortunately, we cannot give such answers without much discussion. Therefore, let us examine some aspects of our understanding of Tamil literature.
Firstly, if we consider all works written in Tamil as Tamil literature, then we must include even the most trivial writings like advertisements or notices on walls etc., under this category. This is because they have been written using the same language (Tamil) as other literary works. However, nobody considers these kinds of writing as part of Tamil literature. So obviously, not everything written in Tamil can be called Tamil literature.
Secondly, if we take into account only those works which are considered as literary classics, then we face another problem. What criteria should we use to decide whether a work belongs to this category or not? There are many different opinions regarding this issue among scholars. Some people believe that any work which contains beautiful poetry or prose deserves to be included in the list of classical works. Others think that only those works which contain philosophical ideas deserve inclusion. Still others feel that only those works which deal with social issues should be classified as classical. And so forth.
So far, we have seen two ways of defining Tamil literature – one based on formality and another based on content. Both methods suffer from serious flaws. For example, according to the former method, every advertisement posted on a wall could qualify itself as Tamil literature! On the contrary, according to the latter method, almost anything written down might become eligible for inclusion in the list of classical works!
Therefore, before deciding upon any particular definition of Tamil literature, we must carefully study its merits and demerits. Only after doing so, can we arrive at a satisfactory conclusion.
Nowadays, most people agree that both formalism and materialism fail miserably when applied to Tamil literature. Instead, they prefer to adopt a middle path between these extremes. According to this view, while considering a piece of writing as belonging to Tamil literature, we must pay attention to three factors:
1. Its linguistic quality;
2. Its aesthetic value; and
3. Its contribution towards society.

The Cooperative Movement in Sri Lanka is a movement of people who have come together to meet their common needs and aspirations through self-help. The cooperative movement has been instrumental in the development of rural areas, especially by providing access to credit facilities for small farmers.
Cooperatives are voluntary organizations, open to all persons able to use its services and willing to accept the responsibilities of membership, without gender, social, racial, political or religious discrimination.
Cooperative members believe in the ethical values of honesty, openness, social responsibility and respect for others.
Cooperatives are autonomous, self-help organizations controlled by their members. They pursue their objectives according to the principles of cooperation.
Cooperatives provide education and training for their members, elected representatives, managers and employees so that they can contribute effectively to the life of the co-operative.
Cooperatives work for the sustainable development of communities through policies approved by their members.
Cooperatives serve diverse interests of their members and society at large, while being responsive to a concern for community welfare.
Cooperatives build bridges between cooperators and the wider society for advocacy on behalf of the cooperative movement.
Cooperatives function within a democratic framework and operate with transparency.
Cooperatives place emphasis on education, information and communication as means of sharing their experience.
Cooperatives consider appropriate forms of cooperation among cooperatives and groups of cooperatives.
Cooperatives are not profit-oriented but service oriented.

The coconut tree is the most important plant in Sri Lankan life. It provides food, drink and shelter for all people of this country.
Coconut trees are found everywhere in our island. They grow on sandy beaches as well as rocky hillsides. The leaves of the coconut palm provide a natural roof to many houses. The trunk of the tree can be used to make furniture or even boats. The fruit itself is eaten raw or cooked into curries. Coconut milk is made from grated flesh and added to rice dishes such as kiribath (milk-rice) and hoppers. The white meat inside the shell is also delicious when fried with onions and spices. Even the water inside the nut is drunk by some people. In fact, there is nothing that cannot be done with coconuts!
In addition to its culinary uses, the coconut tree has other practical applications. Its fibrous husk can be woven into mats and baskets. The oil extracted from it is used to light lamps. The sap collected from the flower buds is boiled down to produce treacle which is then used to sweeten tea. Finally, the dried shells are burnt to give charcoal which is used to cook food over an open fire.
As you can see, the coconut tree plays a vital role in every aspect of Sri Lankan life. Without them we would not have enough food, nor could we build homes or transport ourselves around the island. For these reasons, the coconut tree should always be respected and protected.
